Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Implementing Basic Character Movement
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Implementing Basic Character Movement

Translate Move and Look inputs into smooth movement and camera control using AddMovementInput, controller rotation, and a movement component. Learn frame-rate independence and safe movement patterns.

What you'll implement
Forward/backward, strafing, and mouse-look that respect player view and collision.
Why it matters
Consistent movement preserves gameplay feel across machines and prevents physics issues like tunneling.
Explore Key Topics
Movement Input
AddMovementInput, forward/right vectors, MovementSpeed.
Camera Look
AddControllerYawInput and AddControllerPitchInput for player rotation.
Frame-rate Safety
Multiply movement by GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds() to make speed consistent.
Runtime flow
Model

APawn
Receives AddMovementInput calls and is moved by a movement component.
MovementComponent
Processes the queued movement and applies collision-aware translation.

screens.title: APawn and AController: Roles in Movement
screens.narratorSegment: Begin with a clear definition: APawn is the actor that can be possessed and moved, while AController is the actor that issues commands and represents the player's viewpoint. The controller's rotation determines where the player is looking; GetControlRotation returns that rotation. When a player moves, the controller's yaw tells us the direction the player expects forward to be. This separation matters because the controller can be independent of the pawn's physics. For example, to move relative to view you ask the controller for its yaw, build a yaw-only rotator, and extract forward and right vectors from that rotation. A common misconception is that the pawn itself 'knows' which way is forward; in most control schemes the controller carries that information. A concrete example: when the player moves the mouse to look right, AddControllerYawInput updates the controller rotation. Later AddMovementInput uses the updated yaw to move the pawn forward in the player's new facing direction. Key takeaway: treat controller rotation as the authoritative intent for view-relative movement and use the pawn primarily to accept movement requests and let its movement component apply physics-aware translation.

keyIdea.text: Controller holds look direction and intent; Pawn receives movement requests and delegates actual translation to a movement component.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › APawn & AController
Definition and relationship

APawn is the controllable actor. AController possesses the pawn and defines player intent, including rotation via GetControlRotation. Use the controller to compute movement directions that feel natural to the player.

Controller
Stores view rotation and processes look input. Use AddControllerYawInput and AddControllerPitchInput here.
Pawn
Receives AddMovementInput calls. MovementComponent processes these into collision-aware translation.
Misconception
The pawn is not the source of view direction
Rely on the controller for view-relative movement; do not hard-code forward as world X unless you intentionally want world-relative controls.
Concrete example
When the player presses forward, sample the controller yaw, build a YawRotation with zero pitch and roll, then extract the forward vector via FRotationMatrix(YawRotation).GetUnitAxis(EAxis::X). Use that vector in AddMovementInput to move relative to where the player looks.
Key takeaway
Use controller rotation as authoritative for look-relative movement; let the movement component handle physical translation.
Check your understanding
If the pawn moves diagonally when you look up or down, what rotation component should you isolate to fix it? Answer: use yaw-only rotation.

screens.title: Using AddMovementInput Correctly
screens.narratorSegment: AddMovementInput is the recommended way to request pawn movement. It queues a world-space direction and a scalar scale value and then relies on the pawn's movement component to process that request. A typical pattern reads the movement axis values, computes forward and right vectors relative to the controller yaw, and calls AddMovementInput twice: once for forward/back and once for right/left strafing. An important implementation detail is to scale by both MovementSpeed and GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds to make movement frame-rate independent. A concrete code example shows these pieces together: first get the MovementVector from the input action, fetch Controller->GetControlRotation, isolate yaw with FRotator(0, Rotation. Yaw, 0), compute ForwardDirection and RightDirection via FRotationMatrix, then call AddMovementInput(ForwardDirection, MovementVector. Y * MovementSpeed * GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds()); and similarly for right. A common error is forgetting delta seconds or multiplying twice; test by locking frame rate and observing movement per second. Takeaway: AddMovementInput expresses intent; the movement component and delta time make that intent consistent and physically aware. Using AddMovementInput Correctly means addmovementinput queues directional intent; multiply by movementspeed and delta seconds so application is consistent across frames.. In practical terms, accumulate movement requests that a movement component will process. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › AddMovementInput
Explanation

AddMovementInput should be called whenever movement input is present. It does not directly teleport the pawn; instead it adds to an input accumulator consumed by the movement component. That design keeps collision and sliding behavior consistent.

Common pitfall
Forgetting delta seconds
If you omit GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds(), movement speed will vary with frame rate.
Key takeaway
Call AddMovementInput with direction and a scale that includes MovementSpeed and delta seconds.
Code example
// In AMyPlayerPawn.cpp
void AMyPlayerPawn::Move(const FInputActionValue& Value)
{
  FVector2D MovementVector = Value.Get<FVector2D>();

  if (Controller && (MovementVector.X != 0.0f || MovementVector.Y != 0.0f))
  {
    const FRotator Rotation = Controller->GetControlRotation();
    const FRotator YawRotation(0, Rotation.Yaw, 0);

    const FVector ForwardDirection = FRotationMatrix(YawRotation).GetUnitAxis(EAxis::X);
    const FVector RightDirection = FRotationMatrix(YawRotation).GetUnitAxis(EAxis::Y);

    AddMovementInput(ForwardDirection, MovementVector.Y * MovementSpeed * GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds());
    AddMovementInput(RightDirection, MovementVector.X * MovementSpeed * GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds());
  }
}
Example scenario
When the player holds forward and the camera looks 90 degrees to the right, pressing forward moves the pawn along the controller forward vector, not world X. This produces intuitive movement tied to view.

screens.title: Computing Forward and Right Vectors from Yaw
screens.narratorSegment: To move a pawn relative to where the player looks, compute vectors that ignore pitch and roll — only yaw matters for planar movement. The pattern is simple: query the controller rotation using GetControlRotation, build a new rotator with zero pitch and roll but the controller yaw, and use FRotationMatrix(YawRotation). GetUnitAxis(EAxis::X) for forward and GetUnitAxis(EAxis::Y) for right. Why this matters: if you include pitch, looking up or down will tilt the movement vector into the vertical axis and the pawn may gain or lose height unexpectedly. A concrete example: a player looks up to admire sky geometry; without yaw isolation, pressing forward would also move upward. A common misconception is that you must transform local actor vectors; instead transforming controller yaw gives consistent behavior when the camera and pawn are decoupled. Takeaway: isolate yaw, compute the two planar axes, and use them as the directional inputs to AddMovementInput so forward and strafing feel correct and stable. Computing Forward and Right Vectors from Yaw means isolate controller yaw, then extract forward and right unit axes with frotationmatrix for planar movement.. In practical terms, use controller yaw to derive planar forward and right directions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Compute Axes from Yaw
Step-by-step
  1. Call Controller->GetControlRotation() to get current view rotation.
  2. Construct FRotator YawRotation(0, Rotation.Yaw, 0) to discard pitch and roll.
  3. Use FRotationMatrix(YawRotation).GetUnitAxis(EAxis::X) for forward vector.
  4. Use FRotationMatrix(YawRotation).GetUnitAxis(EAxis::Y) for right vector.
Common mistake
Including pitch by accident
Always zero out pitch and roll before deriving planar axes unless you intentionally want vertical movement when looking up or down.
Concrete example
If the controller yaw is 90 degrees and the player presses forward, the computed forward vector will point along world Y axis. Using that vector ensures forward input moves the pawn in the direction the player expects.
Check
If forward input moves the pawn up or down when looking up, revisit your yaw isolation step.

screens.title: Implementing Look: AddControllerYawInput & AddControllerPitchInput
screens.narratorSegment: Camera look should drive the controller rotation, not directly mutate the pawn. AddControllerYawInput and AddControllerPitchInput are the provided functions to do that. They add deltas to the controller rotation every frame based on input axis values. In practice you read a LookAxisVector from your Look input action, then pass LookAxisVector. X to AddControllerYawInput and LookAxisVector. Y to AddControllerPitchInput. A concrete example: if LookAxisVector. X is positive because the player moved the mouse right, calling AddControllerYawInput with that value will rotate the controller to the right, and subsequent AddMovementInput calls will use the updated yaw for directional movement. Note the Y-axis inversion option in the input mapping: if you negated mouse Y to invert look up/down, the value passed to AddControllerPitchInput will already reflect the desired direction. A common misconception is that look sensitivity should be handled only in the pawn; handle raw input scaling in your mapping or in a sensitivity multiplier, but keep rotation updates on the controller so the view and input remain consistent. Implementing Look: AddControllerYawInput & AddControllerPitchInput means use addcontrolleryawinput and addcontrollerpitchinput to mutate controller rotation and keep view state centralized.. In practical terms, wire mouse or gamepad look axes into controller rotation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Camera Look
Concept
AddControllerYawInput and AddControllerPitchInput update the controller's rotation incrementally. Use input axis values or a scaled look vector to call these functions each frame input is present.
Practical note
Apply sensitivity scaling in your input pipeline or multiply the axis value before calling the functions. Keep inversion configured in input mappings for consistent behavior.
Code snippet
// In AMyPlayerPawn.cpp
void AMyPlayerPawn::Look(const FInputActionValue& Value)
{
  FVector2D LookAxisVector = Value.Get<FVector2D>();

  if (Controller && (LookAxisVector.X != 0.0f || LookAxisVector.Y != 0.0f))
  {
    AddControllerYawInput(LookAxisVector.X);
    AddControllerPitchInput(LookAxisVector.Y);
  }
}
Example
If you want inverted Y look, apply that modifier in the input mapping so the value provided here is already correct and the controller updates match player expectation.

screens.title: Adding UFloatingPawnMovement
screens.narratorSegment: APawn alone does not process AddMovementInput into movement unless a movement component exists. UFloatingPawnMovement is a lightweight movement component suitable for simple pawns. Add it in the pawn constructor using CreateDefaultSubobject and set a reasonable MaxSpeed. The movement component will collect the AddMovementInput requests and apply a collision-aware translation each tick. This design prevents you from manually setting actor location every frame, which bypasses UE's collision and physics systems and can cause tunneling. A concrete constructor example: include the FloatingPawnMovement header, then in AMyPlayerPawn::AMyPlayerPawn() create the component and set its MaxSpeed. Remember to expose MovementSpeed as a UPROPERTY for designer tuning while the movement component enforces its own MaxSpeed. After adding the component, verify that calling AddMovementInput now results in visible movement during Play. Key takeaway: always ensure a Pawn that expects AddMovementInput has a movement component to interpret those inputs safely. Adding UFloatingPawnMovement means ufloatingpawnmovement or a suitable movement component is needed for addmovementinput to produce collision-aware movement.. In practical terms, enable movement processing and collision-aware translation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › UFloatingPawnMovement
Why add a movement component?
AddMovementInput queues intent. A movement component, like UFloatingPawnMovement, reads that intent and executes collision-aware movement. Without it, AddMovementInput may have no visible effect or you would need to implement manual physics and collision handling.
Safety note
Avoid SetActorLocation for per-frame movement
Directly setting location bypasses collision checks and can cause tunneling through thin geometry at high speeds.
Constructor example
// In AMyPlayerPawn.h include header
#include "GameFramework/FloatingPawnMovement.h"

// In constructor
AMyPlayerPawn::AMyPlayerPawn()
{
  UFloatingPawnMovement* FloatingPawnMovement = CreateDefaultSubobject<UFloatingPawnMovement>(TEXT("FloatingPawnMovement"));
  FloatingPawnMovement->MaxSpeed = 1000.0f;
}
Test
After adding the component, compile, possess the pawn in the level, and verify movement responds to input. If AddMovementInput still has no effect, confirm the component owner is the pawn and it is not null.

screens.title: MovementSpeed vs MovementComponent MaxSpeed
screens.narratorSegment: There are two places movement speed shows up: your MovementSpeed UPROPERTY and the movement component's MaxSpeed. MovementSpeed is the designer-facing scalar you multiply input by to control how quickly the pawn should move in response to input. MaxSpeed on the movement component caps the effective speed and enforces safety. Use both: expose MovementSpeed so you can adjust feel quickly in-editor, and set MaxSpeed to a reasonable ceiling to avoid dangerous velocities that cause tunneling. A concrete tuning workflow: set MovementSpeed to a comfortable walking speed, test movement in collision-heavy areas, then increase MaxSpeed only if your movement system reliably handles higher velocities. screens.title: Frame-rate Independence with GetDeltaSeconds
screens.narratorSegment: Frame-rate independence means movement measured per second remains constant whether your game runs at 30 FPS or 240 FPS. GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds returns the elapsed time since the last frame, and using it scales per-frame movement so the total movement per second stays constant. Practically, you multiply your MovementSpeed by GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds when you compute the scale passed to AddMovementInput. For example, passing MovementVector. Y * MovementSpeed * GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds ensures that adding movement each frame results in MovementSpeed units per second regardless of frame count. A common debugging pattern is to run the game with varying frame rates; if movement feels different, you likely omitted delta seconds. Another misconception: people sometimes divide by delta instead of multiplying, which has the opposite effect. Takeaway: multiply, test under low and high FPS, and ensure your speed tuning uses per-second intuition, not per-frame numbers. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Frame-rate Independence
Why it matters
Without delta seconds, movement accumulates per frame and will vary with FPS. Multiplying by GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds keeps movement proportional to real time.
Quick test
Run with frame limiter enabled and disabled. If speed changes noticeably, you need to apply delta seconds.
Example math
If MovementSpeed is 500 units per second, and delta is 0.0167 seconds (60 FPS), per-frame movement contribution is about 8.35 units. At 30 FPS delta is 0.0333, contribution ~16.65 units; accumulating across frames yields the same per-second distance when delta is used correctly.
Gotcha
Do not divide by delta
Multiplying is correct. Dividing will amplify movement on low frame counts and cause erratic motion.

screens.title: World-Relative vs View-Relative Movement
screens.narratorSegment: Two common control schemes differ only in which axes you use for AddMovementInput. View-relative movement computes forward and right from the controller yaw so the pawn moves in the direction the player looks; this is typical for first-person and third-person games. World-relative movement ignores controller rotation and uses FVector::ForwardVector and FVector::RightVector, making 'W' always move along the world's positive X. This setup is common for top-down games or strategy camera rigs. A concrete modification is to replace the FRotationMatrix-derived vectors with WorldForwardDirection = FVector::ForwardVector and WorldRightDirection = FVector::RightVector and keep the same AddMovementInput calls. The misconception to avoid is mixing the two unintentionally: if you want world-relative controls, remove controller yaw usage entirely. Takeaway: choose the axis source intentionally based on gameplay needs; both are valid, but they produce fundamentally different player experiences. View-relative (Controller)
Compute yaw, derive forward/right via FRotationMatrix(Yaw).GetUnitAxis, then call AddMovementInput. This makes movement orient to camera direction.
When to use
First-person, third-person, or any control scheme where camera direction should define movement direction.
World-relative (Fixed axes)
Use FVector::ForwardVector and FVector::RightVector for AddMovementInput. Movement does not depend on camera rotation.
When to use
Top-down or strategy games where directional input maps to fixed world directions.
Example change
Replace controller-derived vectors with WorldForwardDirection = FVector::ForwardVector and WorldRightDirection = FVector::RightVector when implementing top-down controls.

If pressing forward moves the character relative to the camera unexpectedly, verify whether you should be using world or controller axes.

screens.title: Common Implementation Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Here are common pitfalls to watch for and how to fix them. First, forgetting to multiply by GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds produces frame-rate dependent movement; the fix is to multiply movement scale by delta each frame. Second, using SetActorLocation per-frame to move the pawn bypasses the engine's collision and physics; instead use AddMovementInput and a movement component like UFloatingPawnMovement. Third, not adding a movement component means AddMovementInput may not have visible effect; add create default subobject in the constructor. Fourth, including pitch when computing movement axes causes unintended vertical translation when the player looks up or down; zero out pitch and roll and use yaw-only rotation. Fifth, setting MovementSpeed too high without adjusting MaxSpeed can create tunneling; set a ceiling on the movement component and test in collision-heavy scenes. The concrete habit to form: implement, test at multiple frame rates, and verify collision behavior. This checklist prevents the most frequent movement bugs in early prototypes. Frame-rate dependent movement
Cause: omitted GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds. Fix: multiply movement by delta seconds.
Bypassing collision
Cause: SetActorLocation for continuous movement. Fix: use AddMovementInput and a movement component.

Cause: missing movement component. Fix: CreateDefaultSubobject<UFloatingPawnMovement> in the constructor.
Unintended vertical movement
Cause: using full controller rotation including pitch. Fix: build a yaw-only rotator before extracting axes.
Tunneling at high speeds

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will bring input mappings to life. We'll convert the Move and Look input actions into reliable character translation and camera rotation. You'll learn how the Pawn and its Controller collaborate: the controller represents where the player is looking, and the pawn receives movement requests through AddMovementInput. We will cover frame-rate independence with GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds, computing forward and right vectors from the controller's yaw using FRotationMatrix, and enabling movement processing by adding a UFloatingPawnMovement component. You will also implement AddControllerYawInput and AddControllerPitchInput to let the player look around. Along the way I will point out common mistakes, such as directly setting actor location or forgetting a movement component, and explain why they cause physics and collision problems. By the end you will be able to move, strafe, and look smoothly in a play session, tune MovementSpeed, and test for tunneling and inconsistent speeds. Think about a simple maze scene where movement must feel consistent across machines — that is the practical goal here.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to implement directional movement and mouse look in a C++ APawn, tune movement responsiveness, and diagnose common movement bugs. You will learn to call AddMovementInput correctly and compute forward and right vectors from the controller's yaw. I will show you why GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds is essential for frame-rate independent movement and how adding a UFloatingPawnMovement component enables collision-aware translation via movement components. You'll implement AddControllerYawInput and AddControllerPitchInput to let the player rotate the view, and you'll know when to prefer world-relative movement for top-down games. Each objective connects to a practical step: adding a MovementSpeed property you can tweak in the editor, wiring Move and Look input actions, compiling, and testing in a simple maze level. Finally, you'll learn two common pitfalls to check for: directly setting location instead of queuing movement, and forgetting the movement component. These skills make player movement predictable, testable, and safe in most gameplay scenarios.

This secondary objectives slide focuses on skills you should practice and the debugging checklist you'll use during tests. Practice computing forward and right vectors from the controller yaw and calling AddMovementInput with scaled axis values. Learn to add a MovementSpeed UPROPERTY so designers can tweak velocity in the editor without recompiling. For camera control, practice mapping mouse X to AddControllerYawInput and mouse Y to AddControllerPitchInput, and confirm inversion behavior if you apply a negate modifier in your input mapping. For debugging, create two quick tests: one at locked low FPS and one at unlocked high FPS to validate GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds usage, and a collision-heavy level to detect tunneling. Common fixes include adding UFloatingPawnMovement to the pawn and avoiding SetActorLocation for per-frame movement. These practices make it simple to validate movement feel, fix rotation drift, and ensure that input scales behave predictably across hardware profiles.

Begin with a clear definition: APawn is the actor that can be possessed and moved, while AController is the actor that issues commands and represents the player's viewpoint. The controller's rotation determines where the player is looking; GetControlRotation returns that rotation. When a player moves, the controller's yaw tells us the direction the player expects forward to be. This separation matters because the controller can be independent of the pawn's physics. For example, to move relative to view you ask the controller for its yaw, build a yaw-only rotator, and extract forward and right vectors from that rotation. A common misconception is that the pawn itself 'knows' which way is forward; in most control schemes the controller carries that information. A concrete example: when the player moves the mouse to look right, AddControllerYawInput updates the controller rotation.
